extracted.intended_audience: students, scholars, and writers interested in humor theory (Victorian psychology / relief theory)
extracted.subtask_description: Applying Herbert Spencer's relief theory to analyze or craft comic effects that rely on a transfer of attention from a 'great' frame to a 'small' frame so that mobilized nervous energy discharges as laughter. Useful for scholars of humor and writers seeking a physiological/structural account of why certain comic moves work.

rubrics_metrics.name: Hydraulic premise (nervous-energy discharge)
rubrics_metrics.description: Treat the nervous system as analogous to a steam boiler: emotional and intellectual activity generates nervous energy that must discharge somewhere; laughter is one channel of that discharge.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The page explains this as the physiological foundation for why surplus mobilized energy needs an outlet; when energy gathered for a serious purpose is suddenly superfluous, it may discharge as laughter. Use this premise to justify why shifts in perceived significance produce bodily responses.

rubrics_metrics.name: Defining formula: descending incongruity
rubrics_metrics.description: "Consciousness is unawares transferred from great things to small" — laughter occurs when the mind prepared for something significant discovers the actual object is petty or trivial and the mobilized energy overflows into bodily movement (laughter).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is the central rule for comic construction under Spencer: craft a setup that builds a 'great' frame and then reveal a much lower-level reality. The original wording emphasizes the unconscious transfer and the contrast (great→small). Example: a tender poem ending with a trivial mishap.

rubrics_metrics.name: Direction matters (asymmetry of incongruity)
rubrics_metrics.description: Descending incongruity (great→small) produces laughter; ascending incongruity (small→great) produces wonder, awe, or surprise — not laughter.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The asymmetry is critical for analysis or composition: a ridiculous thing dressed up as something grand is funny; a grand thing emerging from something ridiculous is sublime. Use this to distinguish comedic from sublime/admiring effects.

rubrics_metrics.name: Necessary condition: buildup of attention or emotion at a high level
rubrics_metrics.description: There must be a buildup of attention or emotion at one (higher) level — the 'great thing' frame — before the drop.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When evaluating or writing a comic text, check whether the setup genuinely mobilizes serious attention, sympathy, or expectation rather than merely stating an absurdity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Necessary condition: sudden revelation that the actual object is at a much lower level
rubrics_metrics.description: A sudden revelation must show that the actual object is at a much lower level than the mobilized frame.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The contrast must be marked and revealed abruptly (a 'punchline' or final detail) so that the previously mobilized energy has nowhere serious to go.

rubrics_metrics.name: Necessary condition: no serious affect competing for discharge
rubrics_metrics.description: There must be no serious affect (e.g., fear, love, concentrated effort) capturing the mobilized energy; otherwise that affect will occupy the discharge instead of laughter.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When analyzing humor failures, consider whether competing emotions (fear, pity that remains active, romantic concern) prevent laughter from occurring.

rubrics_metrics.name: Necessary condition: path of least resistance leads to laughter muscles
rubrics_metrics.description: The path of least resistance for discharge must be the muscles of laughter (face, diaphragm, vocal organs) rather than productive action.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Physiological plausibility matters in Spencer's account: if action or other responses are the natural outlets, energy will not discharge as laughter. For comic craft, ensure the situation eliminates productive actions as plausible outlets.

rubrics_metrics.name: Exclusion: simple delight or mere joy are not the same as laughter here
rubrics_metrics.description: Spencer excludes laughter that arises from mere delight or joy, treating those as different physiological events.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not conflate simple pleasure with the comic discharge described by Spencer. If an instance is joyful rather than a redirected discharge, it falls outside this account.

rubrics_metrics.name: Exclusion: ascending surprise/admirative responses are not comic
rubrics_metrics.description: Ascents from small→great produce wonder, awe, or surprise rather than laughter.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use this exclusion to classify effects: when an element is elevated rather than demoted, expect sublime or admiring reactions, not comic ones.

rubrics_metrics.name: Exclusion: no laughter when the 'fall' is into genuine pain
rubrics_metrics.description: If the revealed lower-level condition involves genuine pain, the mobilized energy is captured by the pain and will not discharge as laughter.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In evaluating jokes about mishaps or failures, determine whether the victim's pain is genuine enough to suppress laughter per Spencer's rule.

rubrics_metrics.name: Enduring insight: direction-of-incongruity principle
rubrics_metrics.description: Even after rejecting the hydraulic physiology, the direction-of-incongruity (pomp punctured, the high made low) remains a robust observation: descents from the dignified to the petty are reliably comic across forms.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat this as an empirical stylistic principle for analysis and composition: many comic structures rely on puncturing the grand or dignified to produce humor.

rubrics_metrics.name: Diagnostic questions for applying Spencer's test
rubrics_metrics.description: A set of questions to diagnose whether Spencer's mechanism explains a comic instance: Does the setup mobilize attention/emotion at a high or weighty level? Does the punchline drop the object to a much lower level? Is the descent (great→small), not the ascent (small→great)? Is there mobilized energy with no serious outlet, available to discharge as laughter?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use these questions as a checklist when evaluating or crafting comic material to see whether the relief/discharge account plausibly applies; they operationalize the necessary conditions above.
